query: FeNiCrCoCu is considered suitable for thin-film use, and its expense favors applying it as a protective coating on conventional metals rather than using it in bulk. Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior in relation to coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but largely addressed the alloy itself or a limited thermal regime rather than the overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures. Under the constraints that FeNiCrCoCu remains a thin protective coating and that high-temperature wear is the target application, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs its overall wear resistance and why? Specify an intervention relative to a baseline coating condition, predict the observations expected if the hypothesis is correct, state the applicable temperature and loading boundaries, connect the hypothesis to prior evidence, and identify a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment of the FeNiCrCoCu thin coating induces the formation of an adherent, mechanically robust oxide/diffusion layer at the contact surface that governs high‐temperature wear resistance by reducing friction and mitigating abrasive damage.
generation.material_initial_state: FeNiCrCoCu thin protective coating deposited on a conventional metal substrate without any pre-formed surface modification.
generation.intervention: Apply a controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment (or slight compositional tuning to encourage in situ oxide formation) prior to wear testing.
generation.conditions: High-temperature wear tests conducted in the range of 500–700°C under realistic tribological loading, with the untreated coating serving as the baseline.
generation.structural_mediator: A uniform, adherent oxide/diffusion layer (potentially containing spinel-like phases) formed at the coating’s surface.
generation.mechanism: The pretreated coating forms a protective oxide/diffusion layer that acts as a lubricious barrier, reducing direct metal–metal contact and mitigating abrasive wear processes under high-temperature conditions.
generation.predicted_outcome: If the hypothesis is correct, the pre-treated coating should show a significantly lower friction coefficient and reduced wear rate compared to the untreated baseline. Microstructural analyses (e.g., SEM, EDS, XRD) will reveal a continuous, robust oxide/diffusion layer at the contact surface that correlates with improved wear performance.
generation.baseline: FeNiCrCoCu coating without the thermal oxidation pretreatment, tested under the same high-temperature and loading conditions.
generation.boundary: The effect is expected under high-temperature conditions (500–700°C) with realistic tribological loads; the improvement mechanism may not manifest at room temperature or under very low loading conditions.
generation.uncertainty: The exact magnitude of wear rate reduction and the detailed phase composition of the protective layer may vary with the oxidation parameters. Long-term cyclic behavior and durability of the oxide layer under extended service conditions remain to be fully characterized.

falsification_experiment.design: Prepare two sets of FeNiCrCoCu coatings on conventional metal substrates. Subject one set to a controlled thermal oxidation pretreatment (e.g., heating at 650°C for 1 hour in a controlled oxygen atmosphere) to promote oxide/diffusion layer formation, while keeping the other set untreated. Then, perform high-temperature wear tests (500–700°C) under identical tribological loading conditions. After testing, evaluate the friction coefficients, wear rates, and examine the surface microstructure (using SEM, EDS, XRD) to determine the presence and integrity of the oxide/diffusion layer.
measurements: Microstructural analysis (SEM, EDS, XRD) of the wear surface
Adhesion strength of the oxide/diffusion layer (if applicable)
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the pre-treated coatings do not show statistically significant improvements (i.e., similar friction coefficients and wear rates) compared to the untreated coatings, and if microstructural analysis fails to reveal a continuous and robust oxide/diffusion layer, then the hypothesis—that the controlled formation of such a layer governs high-temperature wear resistance—will be falsified.

cited_evidence.text: Abstract In this paper, the Si-20Cr-20Fe coating was prepared on MoNbTaTiW RHEA by a fused slurry method. The microstructural evolution and compositions of the silicide coating under high-temperature oxidation environment were studied. The results show that the silicide coating could effectively prevent the oxidation of the MoNbTaTiW RHEA. The initial silicide coating had a double-layer structure: a high silicon content layer mainly composed of MSi 2 as the outer layer and a low silicon content layer mainly contained M 5 Si 3 as the inner layer. Under high-temperature oxidation conditions, the silicon element diffused from the silicide coating to the RHEA substrate while the oxidation of the coating occurred. After oxidation, the coating was composed of an outer oxide layer and an inner silicide layer. The silicide layer moved toward the inside of the substrate, led to the increase of its thickness. Compared with the initial silicified layer, its structure did not change significantly. The structure and compositions of the oxide layer on the outer surface strongly depended on the oxidation temperature. High-entropy alloys (HEAs) present a new approach of alloying concepts. Whereas conventional alloys usually comprise one major alloying element and minor additions of other alloying elements to improve properties, HEAs consist of at least five elements with close to equimolar composition. For several compositions, the desired formation of solely solid solutions with a face-centred cubic (fcc) or a body-centred cubic (bcc) structure could be achieved [ [1] , [2] , [3] ].

Several groups of HEAs have been intensively investigated. The term compositionally complex alloys (CCAs) was introduced for HEAs with a multiphase microstructure [ [4] ]. Several investigations prove the formation of primarily cubic phases in the alloy AlCoCrCuFeNi and its derivatives [ [5] , [6] , [7] ]. Aluminium strongly influences the microstructure, phase formation and resulting properties. Furthermore, aluminium acts as a stabiliser of bcc solid solutions and can suppress the formation of complex phases [ [8] , [9] , [10] ]. frame.system: FeNiCrCoCu thin-film protective coating applied on conventional metal substrates
frame.goal: To mechanistically explain and predict the overall wear resistance at high temperatures by identifying the key process that governs wear behavior compared to room-temperature conditions.
frame.limitation: Previous studies focused on room-temperature wear and limited thermal regimes, leaving the overall high-temperature wear mechanism of the coating underexplored.
root_cause_cues: overall wear response of a coating across different temperatures
high-temperature wear is the target application
constraints: FeNiCrCoCu must remain a thin protective coating
the intervention and tests must be relevant to high-temperature wear conditions
frame.regime: High-temperature conditions (e.g., 500–700°C) under realistic loading/contact pressures appropriate for tribological stress, with a baseline room-temperature condition for comparison.
prior_attempts: Earlier studies examined room-temperature wear behavior, evaluating the effects of coating–substrate combinations, composition, and grain size, but did not extend to capture the overall high-temperature wear response.
frame.hypothesis: Under high-temperature wear conditions, the formation and evolution of protective oxide and diffusion layers at the coating's surface govern the overall wear resistance. Specifically, a controlled pre-oxidation or thermally induced interfacial bonding process stabilizes the contact surface by forming a mechanically robust and lubricious layer that mitigates direct metal–metal interaction and abrasive mechanisms.
frame.intervention: Pre-treat the FeNiCrCoCu coating with a controlled thermal oxidation step (or slight compositional tuning to promote in situ oxide formation) before subjecting it to high-temperature wear tests. Compare the behavior of this treated coating against an untreated baseline coating.
frame.predicted_observations: If the hypothesis is correct, the pre-treated coating should exhibit lower friction coefficients and reduced wear rates at high temperatures relative to the untreated baseline. Microstructural analysis would show a uniform, adherent oxide/diffusion layer at the contact surface, correlating with improved mechanical stability under load. Failure of the coating via rapid delamination or increased debris formation would indicate a deviation from the hypothesized mechanism.
frame.falsification_criterion: If high-temperature wear tests reveal no significant improvement in wear resistance, friction coefficient, or microstructural stability (i.e., absence or poor formation of the protective layer) when comparing the pre-treated coating with the baseline, then the hypothesis would be falsified.

decision.trend: Early experiments in high-entropy alloy coatings focused on characterizing wear at room temperature – by adjusting substrate combinations, composition, and grain size – and later studies (e.g., PMC7515071) extended wear tests to elevated temperatures. These works observed that at higher temperatures, an in situ formed oxide (or diffusion) layer can form at the contact surface, lowering friction and wear rates. However, while these studies documented that oxide phases (e.g., spinel in AlCoCrFeNiTi0.5) correlate with improved wear behavior, they did not specifically control or pre-tailor the formation of such layers on coatings like FeNiCrCoCu.
decision.unsolved: For FeNiCrCoCu used as a thin-film protective coating at high temperatures, the key unresolved issue is whether a controlled pre-oxidation or interfacial bonding treatment can reliably produce a protective, mechanically robust and lubricious oxide/diffusion layer that governs wear resistance. The challenge remains to precisely link the controlled formation of the interfacial layer with the observed improvement in high-temperature wear performance, especially under realistic tribological loads and temperature boundaries.
decision.lever: Implement a controlled thermal oxidation pre-treatment (or slight compositional tuning to promote in situ oxide formation) on FeNiCrCoCu coatings prior to high-temperature wear testing. Parameters such as oxidation temperature, duration, and atmosphere should be varied to optimize the formation of an adherent, uniform oxide/diffusion layer.
decision.why: This approach follows the trend in earlier studies that noted beneficial correlations between oxide layer formation and improved wear resistance at elevated temperatures. By deliberately engineering the protective layer prior to testing, the experiment directly tests the mechanistic hypothesis that the formation and evolution of a stable oxidation/diffusion layer is the dominant factor in governing high-temperature wear resistance. If the treated coatings show significantly reduced friction coefficients and wear rates – and if microstructural analysis confirms the formation of the targeted layer – the hypothesis would be supported; otherwise, it would be falsified.
